projects.title: How to merge PDF files

globals.message: How to merge PDF files on Windows
globals.arc: Contrast → App opens → Pick the tool → Drop the input → The app reads it → Choose options → Run it → Job Queue running → Job done → Caveat → Endcard

frames.title: Contrast backdrop
frames.scene: Two tiles, "A web merger" and "On your machine", lit one at a time, then the verdict chip "A contract is a decision worth making on purpose"
frames.voiceover: Four separate PDFs, and the form you are filling in accepts exactly one attachment. To merge PDF files the first search result wants you to upload all four to a server you have never heard of. For a contract or a payslip, that is a decision worth making on purpose rather than by default.
frames.narrative: 0.00s – 22.13s, beats 1, 2, 3 (`bg-contrast`, backdrop declaration 1). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: App opens
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: app opens
frames.voiceover: BizTray is the small icon down in your system tray. Click it and the window opens.
frames.narrative: 22.13s – 28.45s, beats 4 (`app-open`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Pick the tool
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: pick the tool
frames.voiceover: Open PDF Organizer, the sixth one in the list of utilities on the left.
frames.narrative: 28.45s – 34.40s, beats 5 (`app-pick`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Drop the input
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: drop the input
frames.voiceover: Drag all four PDFs onto the drop zone in the middle of the window at once. The order you drop them in is the order they combine in, so drop them in the order you want.
frames.narrative: 34.40s – 45.42s, beats 6, 7 (`app-input`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: The app reads it
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: the app reads it
frames.voiceover: The drop zone becomes a page grid. Sixteen pages here, across the files it picked up. Every page is a thumbnail, numbered, so you can see straight away whether a file came in upside down.
frames.narrative: 45.42s – 59.30s, beats 8, 9 (`app-read`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Choose options
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: choose options
frames.voiceover: The grid is the control. Click a page to select it, ctrl for several, shift for a range. Drag a thumbnail to move it. That is how you fix an order you got wrong on the way in. If the last file should have been second, drag its block up and the numbering follows. Nothing has changed on disk yet. The grid is a plan, not an edit.
frames.narrative: 59.30s – 84.37s, beats 10, 11, 12, 13 (`app-options`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Run it
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: run it
frames.voiceover: Hit the button at the bottom of the panel to write the merged file.
frames.narrative: 84.37s – 88.65s, beats 14 (`app-run`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Job Queue running
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: job queue running
frames.voiceover: Job Queue shows it working. Merging is fast because the pages are copied, not re-encoded.
frames.narrative: 88.65s – 95.82s, beats 15 (`app-queue`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Job done
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, PDF Organizer: job done
frames.voiceover: Done. One PDF containing all sixteen pages, written next to the originals. The four source files are untouched, so a merge you got wrong costs you nothing.
frames.narrative: 95.82s – 109.53s, beats 16, 17 (`app-done`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Caveat backdrop
frames.scene: Claim "Merges any number of PDFs into one, in the order you set", a bar that hits a red stop, then the limit and its consequence and the workaround badge
frames.voiceover: Merging copies the pages as they are. It does NOT re-number anything. Which means if each of the four documents had its own printed page numbers, the merged file counts to four and starts again. PDF Tools adds a fresh set of page numbers across the whole document, which is the usual second step on a report.
frames.narrative: 109.53s – 133.02s, beats 18, 19, 20 (`bg-caveat`, backdrop declaration 2). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Endcard
frames.scene: BizTray endcard: app window on its Job Queue, tagline, wordmark, download button and claims
frames.voiceover: So that is four PDFs dropped in, the order fixed on the grid, and one merged document written out. All of it on your own machine, and nothing uploaded anywhere.
frames.narrative:
133.02s – 147.43s, beats 21, 22 (`logo`). Eases in over the first half of the shot, then holds.

---

How to merge PDF files on your own Windows PC, without uploading a contract to a server you have never heard of.

The first search result wants all four documents on its servers, free up to a limit and watermarked on the way out. None of that is necessary. When you combine pdf files the pages are copied as they are, so nothing is re-numbered: four documents that each started at page one now count to four and start again. Stamping a fresh sequence is the usual second step.

projects.title: How to open a PPTX file without PowerPoint

globals.message: How to open a PPTX file without PowerPoint
globals.arc: Cold-open → Contrast → Mechanism → Drop the input → Choose options → Run it → Job done → Caveat → Endcard
globals.audience: YouTube searchers asking "open pptx without powerpoint"

frames.title: Cold-open backdrop
frames.scene: The .pptx card, and the advice that did not work struck through: "Buy PowerPoint for six slides", "Install an office suite"
frames.voiceover: A deck arrives as PPTX and there is no PowerPoint on the machine. Nine times out of ten you are not going to present it. You are going to read it once. To open a PPTX file without PowerPoint, that distinction is the whole answer.
frames.narrative: 0.00s – 17.93s, beats 1, 2, 3 (`bg-scene`, backdrop declaration 1). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Contrast backdrop
frames.scene: Two tiles, "LibreOffice Impress" and "PowerPoint Online", lit one at a time, then the verdict chip "Presenting or editing? One of these two"
frames.voiceover: If you do need to present or edit, LibreOffice Impress is free and offline, and PowerPoint Online is free with an account. Impress will move some animations and occasionally a font. Online renders perfectly and uploads the file.
frames.narrative: 17.93s – 34.97s, beats 4, 5 (`bg-contrast`, backdrop declaration 2). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Mechanism backdrop
frames.scene: Stations on a rail with packets running: A stack of pages → Opens anywhere → Nothing to edit
frames.voiceover: But for reading, a slide deck is a stack of pages. PDF is exactly that, and every machine opens one. It also cannot be accidentally edited, and it will look identical on the recipient's screen. For circulating a deck rather than working on it, PDF is genuinely better than the original.
frames.narrative: 34.97s – 56.00s, beats 6, 7, 8 (`bg-mechanism`, backdrop declaration 3). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Drop the input
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, Office to PDF: drop the input
frames.voiceover: Open Office to PDF, the first utility in the list on the left. Drop the deck onto the drop zone in the middle of the window. A folder of them works the same way.
frames.narrative: 56.00s – 68.23s, beats 9, 10 (`app-input`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Choose options
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, Office to PDF: choose options
frames.voiceover: Under Output, One PDF each keeps the decks separate. Merge into one stacks several into a single document. Then Quality. Print embeds the images at full resolution. Screen compresses them, which matters on a deck full of photographs. Archive is the long term one. I take Print for anything being sent on, and Screen only when the file has to fit an email limit.
frames.narrative: 68.23s – 96.12s, beats 11, 12, 13, 14 (`app-options`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Run it
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, Office to PDF: run it
frames.voiceover: Hit Convert to PDF, the button at the bottom of the panel.
frames.narrative: 96.12s – 100.50s, beats 15 (`app-run`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Job done
frames.scene: BizTray on the Windows desktop, Office to PDF: job done
frames.voiceover: Done. One page per slide, opening in the browser that is already on the machine.
frames.narrative: 100.50s – 107.87s, beats 16 (`app-done`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Caveat backdrop
frames.scene: Claim "Turns any deck into a PDF every machine can open", a bar that hits a red stop, then the limit and its consequence and the workaround badge
frames.voiceover: A PDF is a stack of pages, so everything that made it a presentation is gone. Which means animations, transitions, embedded video and the speaker notes do not come across. On a deck where the build order carried the argument, the PDF reads oddly. And you cannot edit it back into a deck. If somebody needs to change a slide, they need the PPTX and a real editor.
frames.narrative: 107.87s – 136.82s, beats 17, 18, 19, 20 (`bg-caveat`, backdrop declaration 4). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Endcard
frames.scene: BizTray endcard: app window on its Job Queue, tagline, wordmark, download button and claims
frames.voiceover: So it is Impress or PowerPoint Online to present it, and a PDF to read or circulate it. The conversion runs on your own machine, with nothing uploaded anywhere.
frames.narrative:
136.82s – 149.77s, beats 21, 22 (`logo`). Eases in over the first half of the shot, then holds.

---

To open a PPTX file without PowerPoint, decide first whether you are presenting the deck or reading it once.

For reading, a deck is a stack of pages, and converting powerpoint to pdf gives you something every machine opens and nobody edits by accident. For presenting or editing, LibreOffice Impress is free and offline. The catch with a PDF is that everything which made it a presentation is gone: animations, transitions, embedded video and the speaker notes.

projects.title: Can ChatGPT transcribe audio?

globals.arc: Mechanism → Steps → Contrast → Drop the input → Choose options → Run it → Job done → Caveat → Endcard
globals.audience: YouTube searchers asking "can chatgpt transcribe audio"

frames.title: Mechanism backdrop
frames.scene: Stations on a rail with packets running: Whisper → The chat window → Local
frames.voiceover: Can ChatGPT transcribe audio? Yes, and it is good at it, and there are three limits worth knowing first. The company that makes it also made Whisper, which is the model most transcription tools run. So this is not a question about accuracy. It is a question about file size, privacy and format.
frames.narrative: 0.00s – 21.48s, beats 1, 2, 3 (`bg-mechanism`, backdrop declaration 1). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Steps backdrop
frames.scene: Numbered chips ticking off one per beat: Upload cap, Prose out
frames.voiceover: First, the upload cap. There is a ceiling on the file you can attach, and an hour of uncompressed audio goes past it. Second, it hands you prose. You get the words, not a subtitle file with timings you can use in an editor.
frames.narrative: 21.48s – 38.62s, beats 4, 5 (`bg-steps`, backdrop declaration 2). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Contrast backdrop
frames.scene: Two tiles, "The chat window" and "Local", lit one at a time, then the verdict chip "It wins on everything AFTER the transcript"
frames.voiceover: Third, the recording goes to a server. For a lecture that is nothing at all. For a client call, a medical conversation or an unpublished interview, that is a decision, and it should be a deliberate one. Where it genuinely wins is everything after the transcript. Ask it to summarise the call or pull the action items and it will, immediately, which no local tool here does.
frames.narrative: 38.62s – 65.38s, beats 6, 7, 8, 9 (`bg-contrast`, backdrop declaration 3). One state per beat: the picture steps at each beat start, the loops run on the whole-shot clock.

frames.title: Drop the input
frames.scene: SparkTray on the Windows desktop, Transcriber: drop the input
frames.voiceover: For the transcript itself, open Transcriber, the last utility on the left. Drop the recording onto the drop zone in the middle of the window. There is no size limit, because there is no upload.
frames.narrative: 65.38s – 79.22s, beats 10, 11 (`app-input`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

frames.title: Choose options
frames.scene: SparkTray on the Windows desktop, Transcriber: choose options
frames.voiceover: Model. Tiny through Medium, and you choose rather than being given one. Under Output formats, SRT and VTT are the two you cannot get out of a chat window. That is the practical difference.
frames.narrative: 79.22s – 94.67s, beats 12, 13 (`app-options`). One held shot: the cursor travels 0.42s to its target, dwells, clicks, and the pane settles.

132.27s – 146.17s, beats 21, 22 (`logo`). Eases in over the first half of the shot, then holds.

---

Can ChatGPT transcribe audio? Yes, and it is good at it. The same company made Whisper, which is the model most transcription tools run.

So this is not about accuracy. It is about the upload cap, the recording going to a server, and getting prose back instead of a subtitle file with timings. Where the chat window genuinely wins is everything after the transcript: ask it to summarise the call and it will, immediately. Locally you get audio to text with timestamps and no cap, and nothing after that.

projects.title: What does consent look like?

globals.message: Free software can be paid for honestly, and this is what agreeing to it looks like
globals.arc: Free app → What pays for it → The trade → The promise → Install, settings, uninstall → Recap → Settled → Sign-off
globals.audience: people landing on joinmassive.com who want to know what bandwidth-sharing consent should look like

frames.title: The free utility
frames.scene: A pinned app is clicked on a Windows desktop and the "Video Converter" window opens mid-job
frames.voiceover: [thoughtful] You find a free utility for your PC. A converter, a cleanup tool, a small game. It does the job. It has no trial, no watermark, no account. And somewhere in the back of your mind, you think: what is paying for this?
frames.narrative: Opens on a bare desktop, because finding the app begins with launching it. The pointer clicks the pinned app on "PC." (1.97 s) and the window grows up from the taskbar, then the pointer rests on the job table. The app stays generic on purpose: it stands in for any third-party utility.

frames.title: What pays for it
frames.scene: YOU above four costs; data, ads and subscription in orange, then bandwidth arrives in green
frames.voiceover: Something always is. Your data, ads, or a subscription you forget to cancel. But there is one more cleaner way, that does not touch your data.
frames.narrative: One shot across two beats. The three costs arrive while beat 4 lists them; at the beat 5 boundary they recede and BANDWIDTH arrives in green, the only packet that comes back up the wire.

frames.title: The trade
frames.scene: The consent circuit, USER to NETWORK to REWARD, with the green return arching back to the user
frames.voiceover: Companies pay to read public web pages from a home connection instead of a data center. And software can borrow a little of your internet connection while you are not using it. This is the trade. You spare a little bandwidth for the tool, and nothing to pay. [short pause] But this trade is only fair if you agree to it.
frames.narrative: Orange packets run out along the row, green comes back over the top. The hub cycles six real errands ("Check airline pricing…" through "Check for counterfeit listings…"). Node 02 reads NETWORK, not MASSIVE, by review.

frames.title: The promise
frames.scene: Four empty checkboxes arrive: up front, not pre-ticked, reachable, clean exit
frames.voiceover: So here is what agreeing should look like, step by step.
frames.narrative: Boxes stay empty: this is the promise the next six beats keep.

frames.title: At install
frames.scene: The installer's consent page with the Massive banner; the box starts empty, is ticked, then Next is pressed
frames.voiceover: You see it at install, on its own screen, before anything is running. Not buried in a licence agreement nobody reads. Its own screen, in plain words. Nothing is ticked for you. You reach out and choose it.
frames.narrative: The disclosure paragraph is shown, not narrated, and is verbatim from the source. The box ticks on "You" of "You reach out" (65.46 s), never under "Nothing is ticked for you". Next is disabled until then and is pressed on "choose".

frames.title: A switch you can reach
frames.scene: The app's settings; the "Share idle bandwidth" switch goes off and converting becomes unavailable
frames.voiceover: [short pause] If you change your mind, you can switch the bandwidth on and off.
frames.narrative: The switch goes off on "switch". The copy then reads "Off. Converting is unavailable.": the honest consequence, not a claim that the tool keeps working.

frames.title: Clean exit
frames.scene: Windows' Installed apps page; the overflow menu opens, Uninstall is pressed, the row collapses to "0 apps found"
frames.voiceover: [thoughtful] And when you are done with it, you can uninstall the app. Everything goes with it. No leftover service, nothing running afterwards.
frames.narrative: Menu opens on "uninstall", Uninstall is pressed on "Everything", the row leaves on "goes".

frames.title: The recap
frames.scene: The same four checkboxes, ticked in turn by the pointer
frames.voiceover: Told up front, nothing pre-ticked, a switch you can reach, and a clean uninstall.
frames.narrative: Each tick lands on the phrase that names it.

frames.title: Settled
frames.scene: A green ring closes around the user, four ticks on it, and breathes
frames.voiceover: [short pause] Free software can be paid for honestly. This is what it looks like when it is.
frames.narrative: The sparsest frame in the film and no orange at all: the trade, done properly, settles.

frames.title: Sign-off
frames.scene: The Massive logo on the grid plate
frames.narrative: Silent, after the last line, so the take is untouched. Fades up and holds; the film's 8-frame tail fade takes it out. No URL: the page this plays on is joinmassive.com.
